title: In many real-world datasets, about 30% of numbers start with a 1
body: Benford’s law says that in data spanning several orders of magnitude, like populations, river lengths or stock prices, leading digits aren’t evenly spread: 1 comes first about 30% of the time and 9 less than 5%. It happens because such values tend to be spread evenly on a logarithmic scale, where the stretch from 1 to 2 is far wider than from 9 to 10. Because invented numbers often break the pattern, auditors use it to help spot suspicious figures.

slides.heading: How often each leading digit turns up under Benford’s law
slides.note: Digits 6, 7 and 8 fall in between: 6.7%, 5.8% and 5.1%.

slides.question: Why do so many real-world numbers start with a 1?
options: Small numbers are simply more common
Values spread evenly on a log scale
slides.explanation: Data spanning several orders of magnitude tends to be spread evenly on a logarithmic scale, where the stretch from 1 to 2 is far wider than from 9 to 10.

slides.heading: Does it follow Benford’s law?
slides.explanation: Prices, addresses and bills spread over several orders of magnitude. Heights cluster in a narrow range, and phone numbers are assigned, not measured.
